newsitem.title: USA: Delta names outsider Mullin as chief executive.
newsitem.headline: Delta names outsider Mullin as chief executive.

text.p: Delta Air Lines Inc. chose an outsider as its president and chief executive officer for the first time Friday, naming Unicom Corp. Vice Chairman Leo Mullin to both top jobs at the carrier.

The appointment, which ended a three-month search to replace retired Chairman, CEO and President Ron Allen, raised hopes on Wall Street that the nation's No. 3 airline would finally address nagging problems posed by low employee morale and a poor customer service record.

The chairmanship went to former Western Airlines CEO Gerald Grinstein, a Delta director who is widely believed to have forced Allen's decision to retire after 33 years with the carrier. Grinstein led the search committee to find a new CEO.
Maurice Worth, who had been acting CEO since Allen stepped down July 31, was named chief operating officer.
"Leo Mullin is a strategic and proven leader, and he knows how to build businesses," Grinstein said in a statement.
"His career in customer service industries, with its emphasis on strategic and financial planning, will help Delta focus on creating new opportunities and new value for shareowners."

Mullin, 54, was described as a skilled corporate strategist. As vice chairman of Unicom, the Chicago-based parent of Commonwealth Edison, he has led the electic utility's efforts to expand its unregulated businesses.

He also was credited with helping to return the Conrail system to profitability in the early 1980s. Mullin later served as president and chief operating officer of First Chicago Corp. from 1993 to 1995, losing his job when the bank holding company was bought by Detroit-based NBD Corp.
A recent issue of BusinessWeek magazine named the former McKinsey & Co. consultant as one of 20 all-star CEOs-in-waiting.

"Delta is in great financial shape. It is a powerful competitor in major world markets, and I am impressed with the company's people, plans and strategies," Mullin said. "A top priority will be to see Delta's true worth reflected in increased value for shareowners."

Under Allen's leadership, Delta returned to profitability from huge losses in the early 1990s after undergoing a massive cost-cutting program that raised operating efficiencies and trimmed 15,000 jobs from the airline's payroll.

But the three-year program also devastated Delta's once-vaunted corporate culture, undermined morale at the 60,000-employee company and eliminated many veteran customer service agents. As a result, the airline has been beset by drooping morale and surging customer complaints.
Mullin told Reuters he would seek greater balance between cost-controls and customer satisfaction while trying to rebuild Delta's service reputation.

"When any organization has such a relentless attention to cost ... sometimes the balance can get out of whack. And my hypothesis would be that that's what's happened here and we just bring it back a little," he said in an interview.
"At the same time, we have to continue to pay attention to efficiency because it's the equation of customer satisfaction and efficiency that yields maximum shareholder value."
Wall Street analysts were confident Mullin would be able to reinvigorate Atlanta-based Delta. But they also acknowledged that the challenges awaiting him would be formidable.

"You can point to Continental and United (Airlines) to show how outsiders have really worked in terms of improving a company's performance. And I do expect the same to happen at Delta," said Susan Donofrio, an airline analyst at NatWest Securities Corp. in New York.
"I think he's going to breathe new life into Delta and really bring new ideas to the table, which is something Delta needs," she added.
Delta fell 6 cents to $87.69 on the New York Stock Exchange at mid-afternoon.
